title: Planning Assets, Hardware, Software & File Management
description: Identifying assets needed for a media product, the hardware and software used, file formats and good file management.
content_html:
Identifying the Assets You Need

Before any media product can be created, a producer must identify every asset that will be needed. Assets fall into several categories: images (photographs, illustrations, icons); audio (background music, sound effects, voiceover recordings); video clips (footage, screen recordings); graphics (logos, charts, diagrams); and text (copy, captions, headings). Listing all required assets at the planning stage prevents the common problem of reaching the editing phase and discovering that a critical file is missing, unavailable or in the wrong format.

For each asset, a creator should note: what the asset is; whether it will be created from scratch, sourced from a stock library, or provided by the client; who is responsible for obtaining or creating it; and any legal considerations such as copyright or licence requirements. This asset list becomes part of the pre-production documentation and helps ensure the project remains on schedule.

Hardware and Software for Asset Creation

Different asset types require different hardware and software. A digital camera or smartphone is used to capture photographs; a microphone and audio interface capture high-quality audio; a graphics tablet allows artists to draw digitally; a scanner converts physical drawings into digital files; and a powerful computer is needed for video rendering. Choosing the right hardware for the job affects the quality and speed of asset creation.

Software choices are equally important. Common applications include: Adobe Photoshop or GIMP for editing still images; Adobe Illustrator or Inkscape for creating vector graphics; Adobe Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve for video editing; Audacity or Adobe Audition for audio editing; and Canva or Adobe InDesign for layout and publication design. Each application is specialised for a particular type of asset; using the wrong tool can lead to poor-quality outputs or unnecessary file conversions.

Key Fact

For the exam, you need to know the correct hardware and software pairing for common asset types: still images (camera/scanner + Photoshop/GIMP); audio (microphone + Audacity/Audition); vector graphics (graphics tablet + Illustrator/Inkscape); video (video camera + Premiere Pro/DaVinci Resolve); publication layout (computer + InDesign/Canva).

Understanding file formats is essential for saving and sharing assets correctly. For images: JPEG (lossy compression, small file size, best for photographs on the web); PNG (lossless, supports transparency, best for logos and graphics with sharp edges); GIF (lossless, supports simple animation, limited to 256 colours, best for short looping web animations); TIFF (lossless, very large files, used in print production where maximum quality is needed). For audio: MP3 (lossy compression, small file size, good for web streaming and podcasts); WAV (uncompressed, very large files, used in professional audio production where editing quality matters). For video: MP4 using the H.264 codec (efficient lossy compression, widely compatible, standard for web and social media delivery). For print-ready documents and layouts: PDF (preserves formatting across all devices and print setups). Choosing the correct format depends on the intended use: web delivery favours small, compressed files; professional editing and print favour uncompressed or lossless formats.

File Naming and Version Control

Good file naming and version control practices are essential in any media project. File names should be descriptive, consistent and free from spaces or special characters that can cause compatibility problems across different operating systems. A sensible naming convention might be: project-name_asset-type_version-number, for example charity-poster_hero-image_v3.psd. Version numbers allow a creator to keep earlier iterations of a file in case a later version needs to be rolled back. Without version control, overwriting a working file with a broken revision can cause hours of lost work.

Key Fact

A sensible folder structure for a media project separates assets by type. A top-level project folder might contain sub-folders named: images, audio, video, graphics, exports and working-files. Keeping all assets for one project in a single, well-organised folder structure ensures files are easy to find, easy to share with a team and easy to hand over to a client at the end of the project.

In a professional context, poor file naming has real consequences. A file named “final2_ACTUAL_v3_USE THIS ONE.jpg” is a common but damaging mistake: if a colleague is asked to use the correct version, they cannot identify it at a glance. Spaces in file names can break web links and script references. Special characters such as & or # can cause errors in some operating systems and web servers. In team projects, file naming conventions should be agreed at the start of the project and documented in the work plan so that everyone applies them consistently. In a school context, clear file names also make it far easier for an assessor to navigate submitted work.
exam_tip_html: File format questions are common and have specific correct answers. Learn the four image formats (JPEG, PNG, GIF, TIFF) and be able to state whether each is lossy or lossless and give one typical use case. The most common mistake is saying PNG is suitable for photographs on the web — JPEG is better for photographs because PNG produces a larger file. PNG is better for logos and graphics with transparency. GIF is for simple web animations. TIFF is for print. If the question asks you to justify your choice, always mention both the purpose (what it will be used for) and a relevant property (file size, quality, transparency support).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Assets for a media product include images, audio, video, graphics and text; each type requires specific hardware (e.g. camera, microphone) and software (e.g. Photoshop, Audacity) to create or edit.
  • File format choice depends on the intended use: JPEG for web photographs; PNG for graphics with transparency; GIF for simple animations; TIFF for print; MP3 for web audio; WAV for professional editing; MP4 for video delivery; PDF for print-ready layouts.
  • Good file management — descriptive naming, version numbering and logical folder structures — prevents lost work, speeds up teamwork and makes it easier for clients and assessors to navigate submitted files.

glossary_terms.definition: A file or resource such as an image, audio clip, video clip, graphic or piece of text that will be used in the creation of a media product.
Physical equipment used to create, capture or output media assets, such as cameras, microphones, scanners and computers.
A system for naming files consistently and tracking changes over time so that different versions of the same asset can be identified, compared and recovered if needed.
A method of reducing file size by permanently discarding some data, which slightly reduces quality but produces much smaller files; used in formats such as JPEG and MP3.

practice_questions.text:
Which image file format supports transparency and is most suitable for a logo to be placed on a coloured background?
A) JPEG
B) GIF
C) TIFF
D) PNG
State two types of asset that a media creator might need to identify during the pre-production planning stage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: images / photographs; audio clips / sound effects / music; video clips / footage; graphics / illustrations / diagrams; text / copy / headings. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why using sensible file naming conventions is important in a media production project.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Simple point (1 mark): e.g. 'so you can find files easily'. Development (2 marks): e.g. 'descriptive file names allow any member of the team to identify the correct version of an asset at a glance without opening every file in a folder'. Further development (3 marks): e.g. add 'version numbers in file names also prevent the accidental overwriting of a working file with a broken revision, which could mean hours of lost work with no way to recover the earlier version'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between lossy and lossless compression. Give one example of a file format that uses each type.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): lossy compression permanently removes some data to reduce file size, which means some quality is lost (the original cannot be perfectly reconstructed); lossless compression reduces file size without losing any data, so the original can be perfectly reconstructed (2 marks for a clear description of both; 1 mark for describing only one). Example (up to 2 marks): JPEG is a lossy format, used for web photographs where a small file size matters more than perfect quality; PNG is a lossless format, used for logos and graphics where sharp edges and transparency must be preserved exactly (2 marks for one correct example of each; 1 mark for one example only or one example with a vague description). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is creating a media product that includes a high-resolution photograph for print, a background music track for a web video, and a logo with a transparent background for use on a website.

Discuss which file format the student should use for each asset and why.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion addressing all three assets: TIFF or high-quality JPEG for the print photograph (lossless or minimal compression needed for print quality); MP3 for the background music web track (lossy compression produces a small file suitable for streaming; WAV would be unnecessarily large); PNG for the logo (lossless, supports transparency, sharp edges preserved). Each choice is justified with a relevant property (compression type, file size, transparency, quality). Answers that acknowledge trade-offs (e.g. JPEG could work for print at maximum quality setting, but TIFF is safer) score higher. Secure (3-4 marks): At least two assets addressed with correct format and brief justification. Developing (2 marks): One asset addressed correctly or formats stated without justification. Emerging (1 mark): A single point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A media student working on a team project has been using their own file naming system, which includes spaces and informal names such as 'background music final.mp3' and 'poster image v2 use this.jpg'.

Evaluate the impact of poor file management on a team media project and justify what a good file management system should include.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): A sustained evaluation identifying specific problems caused by poor naming (spaces in filenames break web links and script references; informal names like 'use this' cannot be read by a team member who does not know the context; no consistent version numbering means earlier working versions are lost if overwritten). Argues convincingly for a good system including: descriptive names without spaces (use hyphens or underscores); version numbers appended to each file; agreed naming convention documented at project start; logical sub-folder structure separating images, audio, exports etc. Counter-argument: for a solo project, less rigorous naming may cause fewer immediate problems. However, for team work and client handover, the investment in file management is always justified. Clear judgement reached with specific reference to the student scenario. Secure (5-6 marks): Both problems and solutions explained with scenario application and some judgement. Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided. Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with minimal development. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which file format uses lossless compression and supports transparency, making it ideal for logos on coloured backgrounds?
Which software application is most commonly used for editing audio files in a media production workflow?
JPEG uses _____ compression, meaning some image data is permanently discarded to reduce file size.
A sensible file naming convention uses descriptive names, avoids spaces, and includes _____ so earlier iterations of a file are never lost.
Match each file format to its most appropriate use case.
right: Background music for a web-based video
A short looping animation on a website
A high-resolution photograph destined for print

flashcard_questions.q: Name four categories of asset that a media creator might need for a project.
flashcard_questions.a: Four common asset categories are images, audio clips, video footage and graphics, each requiring specific hardware and software to create.

flashcard_questions.q: Which image file format is best for web photographs and uses lossy compression?
Which image format supports transparency and is ideal for logos on the web?
Which image format is best for high-resolution print production?
Which audio format is uncompressed and used in professional editing?
Which audio format uses lossy compression and is standard for web streaming?
Which video format is standard for web and social media delivery?
Which file format preserves layout for print-ready documents across all devices?
What hardware is used to capture high-quality audio for a media production?
What does version control in file naming allow a creator to do?
flashcard_questions.a: Recover an earlier working version of a file if a later version is broken.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should file names avoid spaces?
flashcard_questions.a: Spaces can break web links and cause errors in some operating systems and scripts.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between lossy and lossless compression?
flashcard_questions.a: Lossy permanently removes data; lossless reduces file size without losing any data.
